content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper theoretically explains the intuition that simple concepts are more likely to be learned by deep neural networks (DNNs) than complex concepts. Therefore, it gives an explanation of why simple interactive concepts in the data are more likely to be learned than complex interactive concepts. The paper explains several previous works using the proposed framework.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros: it is interesting and new to investigate how low-level sensory inputs like pixels composite to form high-level concepts like the normal variables in causal inference. It is intriguing to use the same framework to explain the robustness of a few previous works. Experiments are comprehensive and include a few representative architectures.
Cons: The biggest concern is the confusing terms are quite different from the literature and some of them are a bit over-claimed. For example, 
1) `the inference logic of a DNN on a specific input sample can be represented as a causal graph' - the inference can be represented as symbolic inference but whether the inference can be interpreted causally requires identification of causal effects. The work can be technically stronger if it can guarantee the identification, given this work's focus is theoretical aspects. There are some old works that need to be cited like CCT [1], which is conceptually the same as the idea of this paper.
2) `It has been proven that diverse outputs of the DNN on all 2^n masked samples can be all accurately mimicked by even a concise causal graph with not so many causal patterns' - it is a bit unconvincing since the graph is reduced and it is a tree as opposed to a normal causal DAG.

[1] Visual Causal Feature Learning
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The narrative and flow are good. The validity of causal claims requires more justifications.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.

content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
Explain the reason why simple interactive concepts in the data are more likely to be learned than complex interactive
concepts.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
*strength: 
1. the topic is interesting, if DNNs really learn simple concepts

*weakness: 
1. the claim that "DNNs learn simple concepts" is very vague and misleading. The paper defines simple concepts as lower interaction terms of base concepts, which is fine but not interesting. Perhaps I can understand a very low-level concept has a lower-order interactions, but how do I know the order of interactions for two complicated concepts? Which is more simple? The order of interactions is something that we cannot understand well, but the simpleness of concepts is something that human can kind of understand. Mapping these two terms is a major weakness.

2. The more serious weak point is that the claim "DNNS MAINLY LEARN SIMPLE LOW-ORDER INTERACTIVE CONCEPTS" is not supported well. The first section's claim "high-order interactive concepts are more sensitive to data variations than low-order interaction" is extremely obvious but not related to the claim at all. Given any polynomial regression model, high-order interactive features are more sensitive to data variations than low-order interaction, but this does not mean polynomial regression model MAINLY LEARN SIMPLE LOW-ORDER INTERACTIVE features. Showing this section is very misleading. 

Again, "verifying the phenomenon that low-order interactive concepts are usually learned faster than high-order concepts" does not support "DNNS MAINLY LEARN SIMPLE LOW-ORDER INTERACTIVE CONCEPTS". Also, the phenomenon that low-order interactive concepts are usually learned faster is not well-supported by the theoretical framework. Therefore, the paper did not support its main claim at all to me.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
*Clarity: the writing is easy to understand, but it relies too much technicality term on a previous work Ren et al.

*Quality: it did not support its claim well. For instance, a sentence in Sec.2 writes "Fig. 5 shows that the
DNN first learns low-order interactive concepts, and then learns high-order interactive concepts.
Such a phenomenon verifies the conclusion that the DNN mainly learns simple interactive concept"
It is clear to me that DNN learning low-order interactive concepts first does not imply DNN mainly learns simple interactive concept. Simple things are usually learned first, that does not mean the model mainly learn simple things.
The only thing the author proved is that high-order interactive concepts are more sensitive to data variations than low-order interaction, which is very trivial intuitively. Most claims in the paper are not well-supported by this theoretical evidence.

*Novelty: the topic is novel but not executed well.

*Reproducibility: seems reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: The main issue is that the paper greatly overclaimed what it formulated, and did not have enough evidence to support its claim.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper builds on the notion that predictions from a neural network can be understood as coming from a causal graph of subset of input variables. It then hypothesises that simple concepts, as defined by parts of the causal graph with small input variables, are key to generalization in different ways. It  shows that these concepts are more stable, robust to noise, and learned earlier during training. It then connects this hypothesis to previous papers analysing related observations between complexity of causal subgraphs and different characteristics of neural networks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
___Strengths____
- Figure 5 is interesting, showing that low-order concepts are faster to learn than low-order concepts. Within it, I also appreciated the wide diversity of architectures and datasets evaluated.
- The importance of low-order concepts, although not fully compelling (for instance the mouth example is described as 3-order but really it has a huge number of pixels with very complex interactions) is interesting and worth exploring.

__Weaknesses__
- This paper relies quite strongly on the interpretation of neural networks as causal graphs. To the best of my understanding reading the paper and skimming the proofs, there is little in this framework that distinguishes neural networks from any other type of learning interpreted under the same framework. Therefore, it is hard for me to appreciate the causal graph interpretation as insightful for the specific advantage of DNNs over non-DNN learning approaches.
- In multiple places in this paper we compare low-order concepts with high-order concepts, saying that the former are better in multiple ways. However, I missed the contribution of the vast differences in number of filters as there are an exponential number of n/2-order concepts compared to 3-order concepts.
- Most proofs were loose, often having imprecise notation and mixing claims, citations, and definitions.
- Gaussian noise is often used to talk about robustness or dataset variations, but it isn't necessarily a good model of either.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
__Clarity__
- The paper should be more self-contained in regards to definitions of concepts and explanation of experiments.
- Proofs and theorem statements need to be more precise IMO. I would solve it in two ways: some things don't need to be mathematized, they are just arguments. Some things can be turned into theorems, but then it is important to separate what we state, how we prove it, and what doesn't belong to either the statement or the proof.

__Quality__
I think the mathematical framework is unfortunately not solid enough, as discussed under Weaknesses. The experiments are better, and I would build on them in future versions.

__Novelty__
The paper seems to build quite strongly on Rem et al. On its own, it's not necessarily a bad thing, but I would make sure to make it clear what the differences between the two papers are.

___Questions__
- In figure 1, why does the output of Y() match the output of v() independently of all real values in each input variable? Does Y have infinite capacity? If so, isn't this decomposition true of any function approximation mechanism (such as a decision tree or k-nearest neighbors)?
- Most interactive concepts have ignorable coefficients US ≈ 0, and not so many salient concepts S have large absolute value of |US|. Where is this proven? 
- In section 3.2 why is pure noise a high-order concept? It doesn't have any pattern by definition.
content.summary_of_the_review: I think the concept and proofs are too ill-defined and the basic premise of causal graph being particularly relevant for DNNs compared to other ML methods is a big drawback. I believe the paper did a pretty good job on the experiments, and I would build on this for a future version, mostly dropping the theoretical aspect of the paper, as I think it isn't easy to defend. If instead the paper sold itself as a richer analysis of phenomena that happens in neural networks, it could be insightful about how these methods work. Finally, I would also make the paper more self-contained; as it stands it references multiple papers that are not that well-known either to define concepts, or to explain their experimental results. One can still do that, but the paper should be more readable on its own.
